newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Viag shares lifted by spate of telecoms news.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Viag shares lifted by spate of telecoms news.

text.p: Shares in Germany's Viag AG ended near record highs on Tuesday, buoyed by news the diversified utility won the fourth German mobile phone licence and by speculation of troubles in a rival telecoms alliance.

Viag shares ended bourse trade on the DAX-30 index at 702.50 marks, up 18.50 marks, having hit an all-time high of 703.50. They continued to trade ahead in afternoon electronic trade, up 4.50 marks at 700 marks.
The German government awarded the fourth mobile licence to E2 Mobilfunk GmbH, the consortium owned by Viag and the British telecoms giant BT Plc.
Viag's shares received a further boost when news emerged that the telecoms alliance between Viag's rival utilities Veba AG and RWE AG and Britain's C&W was in jeopardy.
Analysts were divided on what impact the hectic spate of news would have on Viag, indeed on the overall utility sector.
While winning the licence was viewed as a good thing for Viag generally, it hardly took the markets by surprise.

Peter Antes, utility analyst at Bayerische Vereinsbank, said: "I don't know why the share price was so high, because Viag has been saying for such a long time that it would win the licence. The speculation about problems with Veba's and RWE's alliance with C&W probably helped."
Thomas Deser, utilities analyst at BHF Bank, said: "The announcement that Viag had won the licence hardly came as a surprise."
"Viag's competitors need to reconsider their pricing policies, as Viag has said that as a late-starter it will compete on price," said Deser.
Dealers on the floor of the Frankfurt bourse said one of the larger German banks was a notable buyer in the market, which meant the share rise was backed by worthwhile volumes.
But Vereinsbank's Antes pointed out that telecommunications was still only a very small part of the wide range of activities of the utility companies.

"The bourse keeps overreacting to these announcements, which are essentially small news in the overall picture for these utility companies. For example, a cold winter is far more important for earnings at the utility companies," said Antes.

BHF's Deser said: "As to what sort of influence this will have on the overall group, it is hard to say. However, we don't expect any quick reward from the telecoms sector and it will be some time before Viag's telecoms business moves into the black."
Analysts were also split on whether Viag's move into the mobile sector is a good thing. Vereinsbank's Antes fears the German mobile phone market could be reaching saturation point.
"I am not sure whether there is a need for another mobile telephonic licence -- the market is pretty full as it stands," said Antes.

"Perhaps Viag will bring something to the market in the way of technical expertise. Or maybe it can win market share based on price, but I am not sure if the returns for the company are there on that basis," said Antes.
